# SnapDeck AI

> Turn photos and PDFs into flashcards instantly with on-device AI.

SnapDeck AI is an iOS app that uses Apple Intelligence to generate flashcards from photos of textbooks, lecture notes, handouts, and PDF documents. All processing happens on-device — no internet required, no cloud uploads, completely private.

## Key Facts

- Platform: iOS (iPhone 15 Pro and later, iOS 26+)
- AI: Apple Intelligence (on-device Foundation Models)
- Privacy: 100% on-device, no data collection, no accounts required
- Price: Free (3 decks/month), Premium one-time purchase for unlimited use (no subscription)
- Developer: 12F ApS (https://12f.dk/)
- Website: https://snapdeck.12f.dk/

## Features

- Snap a photo of any study material to create flashcards
- Import PDFs for flashcard generation
- Type or paste text manually
- Interactive study mode with flip cards
- Progress tracking (know it / review it), study streaks, XP and stats
- On-device AI — no internet connection needed
- Dark mode; app available in 39 languages
- No accounts, no tracking, no data leaves the device

## Blog

Study advice for students, published at https://snapdeck.12f.dk/blog/ (RSS: https://snapdeck.12f.dk/feed.xml).

- [How to memorise a lot of information quickly — without the fluff](https://snapdeck.12f.dk/blog/how-to-memorize-quickly/) — study-tips, 2026-07-23. Explains why re-reading feels productive but doesn't build recall, introduces three evidence-backed techniques — active recall (testing yourself), spacing (returning to material at increasing intervals), and good question-writing — and shows how to start with whatever material you have right now, manually or with a photo-to-flashcards tool like SnapDeck AI.
- [The night-before-the-exam survival guide](https://snapdeck.12f.dk/blog/night-before-exam-survival-guide/) — exam-prep, 2026-07-22. An hour-by-hour triage plan for the evening before an exam: spend the first hour deciding what to study (prioritising half-known, high-mark topics), convert material into questions and answer them rather than re-reading, do a final pass on the topics still missed, then sleep properly because sleep consolidates memory.
- [How to take notes you'll actually study from](https://snapdeck.12f.dk/blog/notes-youll-actually-study-from/) — study-tips, 2026-07-08. Four changes that make notes usable as study material: write questions in the margin rather than only statements (the engine behind the Cornell method), photograph slides and diagrams instead of transcribing them, do a five-minute same-day pass to add questions and mark gaps, and convert notes into cards while the material is fresh rather than during exam week.
- [Why cramming feels great and works terribly](https://snapdeck.12f.dk/blog/why-cramming-feels-great/) — memory-science, 2026-06-24. Explains the fluency illusion — re-reading builds recognition, not recall — and the three findings that matter: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, the spacing effect (Cepeda et al., 2006), and the testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).
